items.article: When I first moved to Dubai, I was an early adopter of the city's 'Wow, it's so safe here!' mindset. Looking back, I feel angry that I ever assumed low rates of petty crime meant lack of serious crime too. When I first moved to Dubai , I was an early adopter of the city’s ‘Wow, it’s so safe here!’ mindset. It didn’t take long to get into the habit of casually leaving my handbag on the table on nights out. When a colleague gave me his old TV, he put it on the back seat of my car, where it stayed for a week without being stolen. I took to walking home alone from a night out if I couldn’t hail a taxi – a risk I wouldn’t take in any other city. Looking back, I feel angry that I ever assumed low rates of petty crime meant lack of serious crime too. I now feel foolish that I ever equated my personal safety with replaceable possessions. After all, many men respect objects more than women – as I learned to my cost. Within eight months, I was subjected to sexual assault by a stranger – an attack that reflected my mistaken belief that such things just didn’t happen in the UAE , a view that is widely held to this day. On that particular evening, after my job as a magazine editor, I had a quick drink at a popular pub, before attending a short film festival in an art gallery. items.article: Adding in a second neural network that guesses the identity of hidden pieces was key. Deep Blue took down Garry Kasparov at chess in 1997, AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, and poker bots have been beating professionals for years. But one classic game called Stratego held out. Even DeepMind, with its exceptional budget, couldn’t build a machine that reliably beat the best human players. Now, a team of researchers from Carnegie Mellon, MIT, New York University, and Stanford University has done it. Their AI, called Ataraxos, beat Pim Niemeijer, arguably the best Stratego player of all time, 15 games to one, with four draws. And it took just 16 GPUs and a few thousand dollars to train it. In Stratego , each player gets 40 pieces representing military ranks, from a marshal down to a spy, plus bombs and a flag. You win by capturing the opponent’s flag. Your opponent knows where your pieces are, but not what they are. Identities are revealed only when two pieces collide in battle—the weaker one is removed, and the identity of the winner is revealed. That makes Stratego an imperfect-information game, just like poker, which computers cracked years ago. “There’s something super distinctive about Stratego , which is that it is a massive amount of hidden information that unfolds over a very long time scale,” said Eugene Vinitsky, a researcher at NYU and co-author of the study. items.article: For those employed in arduous solitary work such as cab driving, a marathon phone call is the perfect place to navigate the dislocations of immigrant life Don’t get The Long Wave delivered to your inbox? Sign up here T he question of the week is: “who are Uber drivers always talking to on the phone?” It’s one that regularly surfaces on Reddit threads and social media and even, on a couple of occasions, in the office. It’s not my question (I know who they are talking to), but I think the fact that many people are so baffled by it tells us a lot about the separate worlds we occupy. When you get a cab on a ride-hailing app, the chances that your driver will be on the phone is high. The conversation is almost always quiet, containing pauses so long that it often seems they are actually no longer on a call. But then comes a rejoinder, a laugh, an interjection, and the marathon continues. For anyone of an immigrant background, the question of who they are talking to is absolutely no mystery.
